This document explores the following files:

- `minuteCaloriesNarrow_merged.csv`
- `minuteCaloriesWide_merged.csv`
- `minuteIntensitiesNarrow_merged.csv`

The analysis checks missing and duplicate data, looks at intensity by hour,
compares the calorie files, and plots calories by hour. It also includes
summary statistics and a calorie distribution plot.

All three files contain the same 33 distinct participant IDs. The `Id`
column identifies participants and is not a numerical measurement.

## Load data

```{r setup}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)

data_folder <- "data"

calories_narrow <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_folder, "minuteCaloriesNarrow_merged.csv"),
  col_types = cols(Id = col_character())
)

calories_wide <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_folder, "minuteCaloriesWide_merged.csv"),
  col_types = cols(Id = col_character())
)

intensities <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_folder, "minuteIntensitiesNarrow_merged.csv"),
  col_types = cols(Id = col_character())
)
```

## Missing values and duplicates

```{r quality-checks}
datasets <- list(
  "Calories narrow" = calories_narrow,
  "Calories wide" = calories_wide,
  "Intensity narrow" = intensities
)

for (label in names(datasets)) {
  frame <- datasets[[label]]
  missing <- colSums(is.na(frame))

  cat("\n", label, "\n", sep = "")
  cat("Missing values by column:\n")

  if (any(missing > 0)) {
    print(missing[missing > 0])
  } else {
    cat("None\n")
  }

  cat("Duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(frame)), "\n")
}
```

**Observation:** The three files have no missing values or duplicate rows,
so they appear clean on these basic checks. This does not tell us whether
every participant has a complete record for every minute.

## Intensity by hour

```{r hourly-intensity}
date_format <- "%m/%d/%Y %I:%M:%S %p"

intensities <- intensities %>%
  mutate(
    ActivityMinute = as.POSIXct(
      ActivityMinute,
      format = date_format,
      tz = "UTC"
    ),
    hour = as.integer(format(ActivityMinute, "%H", tz = "UTC"))
  )

stopifnot(!anyNA(intensities$ActivityMinute))

mean_intensity_by_hour <- intensities %>%
  group_by(hour) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_intensity = mean(Intensity),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(mean_intensity_by_hour, aes(x = hour, y = mean_intensity)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Intensity by Hour of Day",
    x = "Hour of the day (0-23)",
    y = "Average intensity"
  )
```

The source files do not specify a time zone. UTC is used as a consistent
parsing convention here, without shifting the clock times in the files.

**Observation:** Intensity is generally higher during the day and lower
overnight, with its highest hourly average around 18:00. These averages
combine recorded minutes across participants; those with more recorded
minutes at a given hour contribute more to that hour's average.

## Compare the calorie files

Convert the wide file's 60 minute columns into individual minute records,
then match records using both participant ID and timestamp.

```{r compare-calories}
minute_columns <- sprintf("Calories%02d", 0:59)

calories_from_wide <- calories_wide %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(minute_columns),
    names_to = "minute_column",
    values_to = "Calories_wide"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    hour_start = as.POSIXct(
      ActivityHour,
      format = date_format,
      tz = "UTC"
    ),
    minute_offset = as.integer(sub("Calories", "", minute_column)),
    ActivityMinute = hour_start + minute_offset * 60
  ) %>%
  select(Id, ActivityMinute, Calories_wide)

calories_narrow <- calories_narrow %>%
  mutate(
    ActivityMinute = as.POSIXct(
      ActivityMinute,
      format = date_format,
      tz = "UTC"
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  !anyNA(calories_from_wide$ActivityMinute),
  !anyNA(calories_narrow$ActivityMinute)
)

calorie_comparison <- full_join(
  calories_narrow,
  calories_from_wide,
  by = c("Id", "ActivityMinute"),
  relationship = "one-to-one"
)

overlap <- calorie_comparison %>%
  filter(!is.na(Calories), !is.na(Calories_wide))

overlap_matches <- all(overlap$Calories == overlap$Calories_wide)

cat("Overlapping minutes:", nrow(overlap), "\n")
cat("Overlapping readings match:", overlap_matches, "\n")

cat(
  "Minutes only in narrow file:",
  sum(is.na(calorie_comparison$Calories_wide)),
  "\n"
)

cat(
  "Minutes only in wide file:",
  sum(is.na(calorie_comparison$Calories)),
  "\n"
)

stopifnot(nrow(overlap) > 0, overlap_matches)

calorie_comparison <- calorie_comparison %>%
  mutate(
    Calories = coalesce(Calories, Calories_wide),
    hour = as.integer(format(ActivityMinute, "%H", tz = "UTC"))
  )

mean_calories_by_hour <- calorie_comparison %>%
  group_by(hour) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_calories = mean(Calories),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

**Observation:** The two calorie files agree on their overlapping minutes.
They also cover some different minutes, so combining the files fills in
additional records beyond either file alone.

## Calories by hour

```{r hourly-calories}
ggplot(mean_calories_by_hour, aes(x = hour, y = mean_calories)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Calories per Minute by Hour of Day",
    x = "Hour of the day (0-23)",
    y = "Average calories per minute"
  )
```

**Observation:** The hourly calorie pattern is similar to the intensity
pattern, with higher averages during the day and a peak around 18:00.
These averages combine recorded minutes across participants; those with
more recorded minutes at a given hour contribute more to that hour's
average. The results describe this dataset rather than everyone generally.

The calorie plot uses the combined calorie files, while the intensity plot
uses the intensity file, so their recording coverage is not identical.

## Summary statistics

Check the distributions of the calorie and intensity readings.
The calorie summary and histogram below use the narrow calorie file.

```{r summary-statistics}
cat("Calories per minute:\n")
print(summary(calories_narrow$Calories))

cat("Standard deviation:", sd(calories_narrow$Calories), "\n")
cat("Recorded minutes:", nrow(calories_narrow), "\n")
cat("Zero-calorie minutes:", sum(calories_narrow$Calories == 0), "\n")

cat("\nIntensity:\n")
print(summary(intensities$Intensity))

cat("Standard deviation:", sd(intensities$Intensity), "\n")
cat("Recorded minutes:", nrow(intensities), "\n")
```

**Observation:** The mean calorie reading is 1.62 per minute and the median
is 1.22. Only 7 of 1,325,580 readings are zero; this check alone does not
tell us whether they are valid or recording artefacts, so they are left
in the analysis.

## Calorie distribution

```{r calorie-distribution}
ggplot(calories_narrow, aes(x = Calories)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "darkorange", colour = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Calories per Minute",
    x = "Calories per minute",
    y = "Count"
  )
```

**Observation:** Most minute-level calorie readings are toward the lower
end of the scale, with a smaller number of higher readings.

## Dashboard requirements

### Functional

- Show average calories and intensity by hour.
- Let users filter results by date and participant.
- Compare calories across intensity scores.
- Combine overlapping calorie files without double-counting; show coverage gaps.
- Summarise participants and recorded minutes for the selected filters.

### Non-functional

- Keep charts and filters responsive.
- Ensure calculations are accurate and reproducible.
- Use clear labels, readable contrast and accessible charts.
- Protect participant data and avoid exposing IDs unnecessarily.
- Keep data preparation and dashboard logic easy to maintain.

The functional requirements focus on the comparisons these datasets support:
how calories and intensity vary by hour, how they relate, and which records
are available for selected dates and participants. Combining the calorie
files is useful because their overlapping values match, but each also
contains minutes not found in the other.

The non-functional requirements help ensure the dashboard remains responsive
and its results are clear, reliable and appropriately protected. Showing
recording coverage helps users avoid interpreting unrecorded minutes as
zero activity.
